fruit-salad-including-citrus-fruits-with.title: Fruit Salad with Citrus and Pudding

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit salad with citrus and pudding is a light dish that combines fresh oranges, grapefruits, mandarins, lime and a delicate vanilla pudding. The blend of sweet and tangy notes makes it a refreshing dessert suitable for breakfast or a light snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Citrus fruits are rich in vitamin C, which supports the immune system.
The pudding base is usually made from milk, eggs, and starch, giving the dish a creamy texture.
Combining fruit and pudding is traditional in Mediterranean and Asian cuisines.
Oranges and grapefruits contain flavonoids that help protect cells from oxidative stress.
Fruit salad can be served chilled or slightly warmed to enhance the citrus aroma.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Citrus fruits provide an excellent source of vitamin C, which boosts immunity and supports collagen synthesis.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from the fruits aids intestinal function and promotes satiety.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids in citrus protect cells from free‑radical damage.

items.title: Calcium from pudding
items.content: Milk‑based pudding supplies calcium essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Low‑calorie dessert
items.content: When prepared with moderate sugar, the salad remains light and suitable for weight management.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to oranges, grapefruits, or lime.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Sugar content in pudding
items.content: Overly sweet pudding increases calories and may contribute to dental caries.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Grapefruit can affect the metabolism of certain medications; consult a doctor if you take prescription drugs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad in individual glasses or bowls, garnish with mint leaves. Optional additions include nuts, honey, or yogurt for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours to maintain fruit freshness and pudding texture.

hot-dog-sandwich-nfs-on-white-bun.title: Hot Dog Sandwich, NFS, on White Bun

content.title: About
content.content: The NFS hot dog sandwich is a classic American fast‑food item consisting of a grilled or boiled sausage placed inside a soft white bun. It is commonly served with mustard, ketchup, mayonnaise, and pickles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first hot dog appeared in the United States in the late 19th century and quickly became a street‑food staple.
The white bun is traditionally soft and slightly sweet, highlighting the flavor of the sausage.
"NFS" (No Frying Sauce) indicates that the sauce is served on the side rather than being cooked with the sausage.
More than 20 billion hot dogs are sold annually in the U.S.
There are many regional variations, from chili dogs to "carne" versions with cheese and bacon.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: A typical sausage provides about 12 g of protein per 100 g, helping to maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat in the sausage supplies iron, essential for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The combination of protein, fat, and carbohydrates offers a quick source of energy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Sausages often contain a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure when consumed frequently.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Traditional sausages are rich in saturated fats, which in excess may contribute to cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Some recipes include dairy, gluten in the bun, and spices that can trigger allergic reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hot dogs are usually eaten by hand, gently squeezing the bun to keep the sausage in place. Add mustard, ketchup, mayo, pickles, onions, or cheese according to personal taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sausages in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C, and consume a prepared sandwich within 2‑3 hours. Keep buns in a sealed bag in a dry place to prevent them from drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Hot peppers, also called chili peppers, are the pungent fruits of plants in the genus Capsicum, native to the Americas. They come in many varieties, from mild jalapeños to very hot habaneros and ghost peppers. Their heat comes from capsaicin, and they are used fresh, dried, and ground to flavor dishes around the world.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The heat of chili peppers comes from capsaicin, which is concentrated in the white membranes around the seeds.
Heat is measured on the Scoville scale, from mild peppers to extremely hot ones.
Birds do not feel the heat of capsaicin, which helps them spread the seeds.
Dairy products such as milk or yogurt can help relieve the burning sensation better than water.
Chili peppers were domesticated in the Americas thousands of years ago and are now used worldwide.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Hot peppers contain a lot of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Contains carotenoids
items.content: Red peppers provide carotenoids that the body can convert into vitamin A.

items.title: Contains capsaicin
items.content: Capsaicin is being studied for its effects on metabolism and satiety.

items.title: Adds flavor without salt
items.content: Spicy peppers add strong flavor, which can reduce the need for added salt.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Hot peppers contain flavonoids and other plant compounds with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Burning and irritation
items.content: Hot peppers can cause burning in the mouth, stomach discomfort, heartburn, or diarrhea, especially in people with reflux, gastritis, or irritable bowel syndrome.

items.title: Skin and eye irritation
items.content: Capsaicin can burn skin and eyes. Wear gloves when handling hot peppers and wash your hands thoroughly.

items.title: Extremely hot peppers
items.content: Very hot peppers eaten in large amounts or in challenges can cause vomiting, severe pain, and other serious problems.

items.title: Allergic reactions and children
items.content: Allergy to peppers is possible, and very spicy foods are not suitable for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hot peppers can be chopped into salsas, sauces, stir-fries, curries, and soups, or roasted, pickled, dried, and ground into chili powder and flakes. Removing the seeds and white membranes reduces the heat. Start with small amounts and adjust to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh hot peppers in the refrigerator in a paper bag or breathable container, where they keep for one to two weeks. Peppers can be frozen or dried for longer storage. Keep dried peppers and chili powder in airtight containers in a cool, dark place.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato chips are thinly sliced potatoes that are deep‑fried until crisp and then seasoned with a variety of flavorings. The “other flavored” range includes creative blends such as barbecue, sour cream & onion, cheese & onion, chili‑lime and more.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial potato chip brand appeared in the United States in 1853.
There are more than 3,000 officially registered chip flavors worldwide.
In Russia, popular flavors include “Crab”, “Sour Cream & Onion”, and “Sweet‑Barbecue”.
Chips are often used in culinary experiments: crushed as a coating, added to salads, or even incorporated into desserts.
Most flavorings are derived from natural extracts, though artificial additives are sometimes used to boost taste.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Potato chips provide quick‑digesting carbohydrates that supply rapid energy.

items.title: Vitamin C content
items.content: When processed properly, a portion of vitamin C is retained, supporting the immune system.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Chips contain potassium and iron, essential for normal bodily functions.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: If made from whole‑potato slices, they can contribute a modest amount of fiber.

items.title: Pleasurable taste
items.content: Moderate consumption can improve mood thanks to enjoyable flavor sensations.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Deep‑frying adds significant calories and saturated fats.

items.title: Salt
items.content: Excess sodium may contribute to elevated blood pressure.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Some flavorings may contain dairy, gluten, or soy ingredients.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Use of partially hydrogenated oils can create trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Certain chips contain artificial colors and preservatives that can trigger sensitivities in some individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chips are typically enjoyed as a snack on their own, with dips (sour cream, ketchup, cheese sauce) or as a crunchy topping for salads, burgers, and sandwiches. For a healthier option, choose baked chips with reduced salt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep chips in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from light. Once opened, transfer them to an airtight container to maintain crispness and prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Semolina is a finely ground wheat meal, light yellow or cream in color. It cooks very quickly and makes a tender, smooth porridge with a mild flavor. Semolina from durum wheat is used for pasta, couscous, and baked goods, and in Russian and many other cuisines it is cooked into semolina porridge and used for baked puddings, casseroles, and dumplings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Semolina is made from wheat, either soft or durum.
Semolina from durum wheat is used to make pasta and couscous.
Semolina porridge is a classic breakfast in Russia and the CIS countries.
Semolina is used in desserts, such as Greek revani and the Indian sweet suji halwa.
The English word semolina comes from an Italian word meaning bran or meal.

items.title: Source of energy
items.content: Semolina provides carbohydrates that are quickly turned into energy.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Semolina from durum wheat contains more protein.

items.title: Contains B vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, niacin, and folate help the body get energy from food.

items.title: Contains selenium and iron
items.content: These nutrients support immunity and oxygen transport.

items.title: Cooks quickly
items.content: The porridge is ready in a few minutes.

items.title: Gluten and allergy
items.content: Semolina contains gluten and is not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten intolerance, or with wheat allergy.

items.title: Fast carbohydrates
items.content: Semolina is low in fiber, so it raises blood sugar faster; people with diabetes should watch their portion.

items.title: Sugar and additions
items.content: Sweet semolina porridge with sugar, jam, and butter is high in calories.

items.title: For small children
items.content: Semolina porridge should be introduced to children on a pediatrician's recommendation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour semolina in a thin stream into boiling milk or water, stirring constantly to prevent lumps, and cook for a few minutes; usually two to three tablespoons are used per cup of liquid. Add it to baked puddings, casseroles, dumplings, and baked goods.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store semolina in an airtight container in a dry, cool place and check it for pests from time to time. Keep cooked porridge in the refrigerator for two to three days.

content.title: About
content.content: Spinach-filled tortellini are small ring‑shaped pasta parcels stuffed with fresh spinach and ricotta cheese. Served without sauce, they let the delicate flavor of the filling and the texture of the dough shine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tortellini originate from Italy, especially the Emilia‑Romagna and Tuscany regions.
The short cooking time helps spinach retain most of its vitamins.
Although traditionally served in broth, sauce‑free tortellini make a light, diet‑friendly dish.
The dough is usually made from eggs and high‑quality flour, giving it a firm bite.
Italy hosts a "Tortellini Fest" celebrating these stuffed pastas.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Spinach is one of the best plant sources of iron, supporting normal blood formation.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Provides protein
items.content: Tortellini deliver both plant and animal protein (from eggs) that aids tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: A sauce‑free preparation contains little saturated fat, making it heart‑friendly.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Spinach adds dietary fiber, promoting regular bowel movements.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: The dough contains eggs, which can trigger allergic reactions in some individuals.

items.title: Oxalates in spinach
items.content: Spinach is high in oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation when consumed in excess.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Adding salt to the cooking water can raise the sodium level of the dish.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat flour dough contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the tortellini hot, drizzled with a little olive oil or butter. They pair well with a light vegetable broth, fresh herbs, or a sprinkle of grated Parmesan.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Dry tortellini keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 12 months. Cooked tortellini should be stored in the refrigerator in a sealed container for no more than 3 days. Discard if any off‑odor or discoloration appears.

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey (NFS) is tender turkey meat obtained from birds raised without added hormones or antibiotics. It has a mild flavor, a slightly sweet aroma, and a firm yet juicy texture. Turkey is popular in diet nutrition because of its low fat content and high protein level.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey is the national bird of the United States and a traditional dish for Thanksgiving.
Turkey meat contains more niacin (vitamin B3) than chicken.
Unlike chicken, turkey breast is lighter while the thighs are darker due to higher myoglobin content.
There are several turkey varieties, including White, Dark, and Lean (NFS – No Fat Supplement).
Turkey can be grilled, roasted, boiled, or used ground in recipes.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: 100 g of turkey provides about 29 g of high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: NFS turkey contains virtually no saturated fat, making it suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey is abundant in vitamin B6 and niacin, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies phosphorus, selenium and zinc – important for bones, immunity and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: 100 g of turkey delivers roughly 135 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight management.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turkey meat.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked turkey can harbor pathogens such as Salmonella. Cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Turkey contains purines, so people with gout should limit consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Turkey can be roasted whole, grilled as fillets, boiled in soups, or used ground for patties, burgers, and stuffing. Sliced pieces work well in salads, sandwiches, and Asian‑style stir‑fries.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh turkey in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Frozen turkey keeps in the freezer at –18 °C for up to 12 months. Thaw frozen meat in the fridge, not at room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: Plain carbonated water is pure drinking water infused with carbon dioxide. It contains no sugars, flavors, or colorants and is suitable for hydration and culinary use.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial method of carbonating water was developed in the early 19th century.
Carbonation can enhance the perception of taste, which is why it is often used in cocktails and soft drinks.
In some countries, carbonated water is served instead of still water as a restaurant tradition.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Like still water, carbonated water helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Moderate consumption may promote a feeling of fullness and aid digestion in some individuals.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Higher acidity can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcer disease.

items.title: Tooth enamel erosion
items.content: Frequent intake may contribute to enamel demineralization, especially if not followed by rinsing with plain water.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink chilled, use as a base for non‑alcoholic cocktails, mixers, and in cooking (e.g., for batters).

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed container protected from light. After opening, consume within a few days.
